Under Indian law, is there an automatic presumption that custodial statements are obtained by compulsion? Is additional diligence similar to Miranda warnings required? If it is shown that a person was compelled to make statements in custody, does relying on such testimony and its derivative use violate Article 20(3)? How does Section 27 of the Evidence Act relate to Article 20(3), as clarified in the case reported at AIR 1961 SC 1808?

Does Indian law presume that statements made in custody are extracted through compulsion? Is there a requirement of additional diligence akin to Miranda warnings? Where it is shown that a person was compelled to make statements while in custody, will relying on such testimony and derivative use offend Article 20(3)? What is the relationship between Section 27 of the Evidence Act and Article 20(3), as clarified in AIR 1961 SC 1808?

In Indian law, no automatic presumption exists that custodial statements are coerced; hence no extra diligence like Miranda warnings is needed. But, if a person proves actual compulsion in custody, does using such testimony and its derivative use violate Article 20(3)? Clarify the interplay between Section 27, Evidence Act and Article 20(3) per AIR 1961 SC 1808.

Is there a rule in Indian law that custodial statements are presumed free from compulsion, thus negating any duty akin to Miranda warnings? If compulsion is specifically shown to have occurred in custody, would the testimony and its derivative use be barred under Article 20(3)? Also, what did AIR 1961 SC 1808 say about Section 27 of the Evidence Act in relation to Article 20(3)?

The legislation falls under Entry 18 of List III of the Seventh Schedule, which covers 'Adulteration of Food Stuffs and other Goods.' It was enacted to curb the widespread evil of food adulteration and serves as a legislative measure for social defence. The Act intends to suppress a social and economic mischief—an evil that attempts to poison, for monetary gain, the very sources of sustenance and well-being of the community. The offence is socio-economic in nature, and its effects on public health are alarming. In Municipal Corpn. v. Mal, Sarkaria J. observed that the Act curbs and remedies the widespread evil of food adulteration and ensures the sale of wholesome food.

This law is based on Entry 18, List III, Seventh Schedule—'Adulteration of Food Stuffs and other Goods.' It is aimed at checking the growing menace of food adulteration and is a social-defence measure. It seeks to suppress a socio-economic wrong: poisoning, for profit, the basic sources of life and community welfare. The dangers to public health are serious and increasing. This offence is socio-economic. In Municipal Corpn. v. Mal, Justice Sarkaria noted that the Act was framed to curb food adulteration and guarantee wholesome food to the people.

The statute relates to Entry 18, List III, Seventh Schedule ('Adulteration of Food Stuffs and other Goods'). It was passed to fight the pervasive evil of food adulteration, acting as social defence legislation. Its purpose is to stop an economic and social mischief—deliberately contaminating food for money, thereby endangering life and community well-being. The impact on public health is growing grave, and the offence is socio-economic. As Sarkaria J. remarked in Municipal Corpn. v. Mal, the Act aims to curb food adulteration and secure clean food for all.

Legislation under Entry 18, List III, Seventh Schedule ('Adulteration of Food Stuffs and other Goods') targets the rampant problem of food adulteration as a social-defence measure. It intends to suppress the socio-economic evil of adulterating food for profit, thereby poisoning the community's sustenance and well-being. This offence has increasingly severe health consequences. In Municipal Corpn. v. Mal, Justice Sarkaria stated that the Act was enacted to remedy the widespread evil of food adulteration and to ensure wholesome food for the public.

More than 100 applications have been filed, many under Section 207 Cr.P.C., only to delay the trial. Though as per P. Ponnusamy v. State of Tamil Nadu, these could be filed only after charge framing, they were filed pre-charge intentionally. The discharge application was not filed to protract the trial. Overall, the appellant is protracting the trial.

It is argued that over a hundred applications—many under S. 207 Cr.P.C.—were filed solely to stall the trial. Even though P. Ponnusamy allows such applications only post-framing of charges, these were deliberately filed at the pre-charge stage to postpone charge framing. The appellant also didn't file a discharge application, again to delay. The totality shows the appellant is dragging the trial.

The submission is that 100+ applications, largely u/s 207 Cr.P.C., were filed just to delay proceedings. Under P. Ponnusamy, they should have come after charge framing, but were filed earlier to push back that stage. No discharge petition was moved either, merely to prolong. Thus, the appellant is the one causing delay.

He says more than a hundred applications, many under Section 207 Cr.P.C., are purely dilatory. Though such pleas are permissible only after charges are framed—per P. Ponnusamy—they were filed before that to slow down the process. The discharge application was withheld to further drag things. The circumstances clearly show the appellant is delaying the trial.
